stories.headline: STOCKS SURGE IN SHORTENED BLACK FRIDAY SESSION AS NVIDIA-LED REBOUND LIFTS S&P 500 1.60%, NASDAQ 100 2.60%
stories.body: In a session cut short by the 1 PM ET holiday close, the S&P 500 jumped 1.60% to 7,297 and the Nasdaq 100 surged 2.60% to 26,726 as Nvidia and other AI-linked names clawed back much of Wednesday's hot-PCE-driven selloff, when Nvidia had swung from an 8% intraday drop to a 4% close.
stories.explain: Thin, pre-holiday volume exaggerates moves in both directions, so a bounce in a handful of mega-cap, high-weight names like Nvidia can lift the cap-weighted Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 far more than an equal-weighted measure of the market would show. The rebound doesn't reverse the underlying rate math from Tuesday's hot core PCE print; it reflects short covering and bargain-hunting after a sharp drop, which is why today's gain coexists with the 10-year yield still sitting near 4.94%.

stories.headline: FED HIKE ODDS HOLD NEAR 90% FOR DEC. 9 EVEN AS STOCKS RALLY, 10-YEAR YIELD STEADY AT 4.94%
stories.body: Fed funds futures continue to price roughly 85-90% odds of a quarter-point hike to 3.75%-4.00% at the December 9 FOMC meeting, with the 10-year Treasury yield holding near 4.94% (+9 bps) even as equities staged today's rebound, showing the bond market isn't treating today's bounce as a sign the inflation picture has improved.
stories.explain: Equities and rates can diverge because they're pricing different things: today's stock rally reflects a mechanical snapback in oversold, high-beta names, while the yield curve reflects the market's read on where the Fed actually sets policy, and that read hasn't changed since Tuesday's hot core PCE. A 25 bp hike would be the Fed's first increase in a cycle that spent most of 2025 cutting, which is why futures markets treat it as high-conviction rather than a coin flip just three trading days after the data that triggered it.

stories.headline: NVIDIA LEADS TODAY'S REBOUND AS HUANG'S DEC. 1 CLOSED-DOOR TESTIMONY NOW JUST DAYS AWAY
stories.body: Nvidia shares led the Nasdaq 100's 2.60% advance, bouncing off Wednesday's close that had capped an 8%-to-4% intraday swing, as the company heads into former CEO Jensen Huang's December 1 closed-door House testimony over alleged ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, with general counsel Tim Teter following on December 2.
stories.explain: A rebound in the shares doesn't resolve the legal and governance overhang; a transcribed, closed-door national-security interview can surface details about Nvidia's China-exposure and security protocols that move the stock independent of any single trading day's price action. With the testimony now just four days out and sitting inside the same window as the Fed's blackout period, Nvidia remains the name most likely to swing the index disproportionately in either direction heading into December 9.

stories.headline: GOLD CLIMBS TO $3,668 AND DOLLAR FIRMS TO 104.01 TOGETHER AS OIL SLIPS 1.59% TO $83
stories.body: Gold rose 1.33% to roughly $3,668 an ounce and the dollar index firmed 0.20% to 104.01, an unusual pairing since a stronger dollar normally makes dollar-denominated gold more expensive for foreign buyers, while WTI crude fell 1.59% to about $83 a barrel on thin holiday-week liquidity.
stories.explain: Gold and the dollar rising together signals investors are buying gold as an inflation and policy-uncertainty hedge specifically, not simply chasing a weak-dollar trade, which matters heading into a Fed decision markets already expect to be a hike rather than a cut. Oil's decline on light post-Thanksgiving volume is more a liquidity story than a demand signal, since a thinly traded commodity market can see outsized percentage moves on smaller order flow than a typical session would produce.

stories.headline: ADOBE: BLACK FRIDAY ONLINE SALES ON PACE FOR $12.9B, UP 9.2% YoY, FIRST REAL-TIME READ ON THE CONSUMER
stories.body: Adobe Analytics' real-time tracking has Black Friday online spending on pace for about $12.9 billion, up 9.2% year-over-year, the first concrete data point on consumer demand since Tuesday's hot core PCE print raised the stakes on whether spending is cooling ahead of the Fed's December 9 decision.
stories.explain: Personal consumption makes up roughly two-thirds of US GDP, so a holiday-weekend spending pace running above last year's growth rate adds to the case that demand remains strong enough to justify the Fed following through on a hike rather than pausing. Because Black Friday data arrives in near-real time while official retail-sales figures lag by weeks, traders use it as an early, if imperfect, signal of the same consumer strength the Fed will be parsing into its December 9 decision.

stories.headline: DESPITE TODAY'S RALLY, NASDAQ COMPOSITE STILL TRACKS FOR ONE OF ITS WORST MONTHS OF THE CYCLE
stories.body: Even with today's broad-based bounce, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite remains on pace for one of its steepest monthly declines since the Fed's cutting cycle began, as November's run of hot inflation prints and rising hike odds forced a repricing of the long-duration AI and chip stocks that led 2025's rally.
stories.explain: One strong session doesn't undo a month-long repricing, because a single day's short covering in oversold names is a different mechanism from the sustained discount-rate increase that drove the decline in the first place. Until the 10-year yield meaningfully retreats or the Fed's December 9 decision resolves the uncertainty one way or the other, days like today are more likely to be rallies within a downtrend than a clean reversal of November's losses.

watchlist: Fed's Dec. 9 FOMC decision — futures pricing ~85-90% odds of a 25 bp hike to 3.75%-4.00% after the hot core PCE print
Jensen Huang's closed-door House testimony — Tue., Dec. 1, with GC Tim Teter following Dec. 2
Nov. nonfarm payrolls, Fri., Dec. 4, 8:30 AM ET — last major data point before the Fed's blackout lifts
Cyber Monday, Dec. 1 — Adobe forecasts $15.1B in online sales, +6.2% YoY, next read on consumer resilience
10-year Treasury yield near 4.94% heading into the Fed's pre-meeting blackout period

deepDive.title: Why a 25 bp Rate Surprise Can Swing a Trillion-Dollar Stock by Double Digits
content: This week gave finance students a clean, almost laboratory-grade example of duration risk in equities. Tuesday's hotter-than-expected core PCE print sent Nvidia swinging from an 8% intraday drop to a 4% close in a single session, then today's Black Friday rally helped pull the Nasdaq 100 back up 2.60% as the stock bounced alongside its peers. Nvidia's actual business — its chip roadmap, its customer backlog, its margins — did not change meaningfully between Tuesday and today. What moved was the market's estimate of the discount rate used to value Nvidia's future cash flows, and that single variable explains more of this week's double-digit swings than any headline about the company itself.

Every stock's price is, in theory, the present value of its future cash flows discounted back at a rate built from the risk-free Treasury yield plus an equity risk premium. A company like Nvidia derives most of its valuation from profits expected five, ten, even fifteen years out, which makes it behave like a long-duration bond: a small rise in the discount rate shrinks the present value of those distant cash flows by far more than it shrinks the value of a utility or consumer-staples stock earning steady cash today. When the 10-year Treasury yield pushed toward 4.94% this week on hardening Fed hike odds, that single number mechanically lowered the fair value of every far-out AI cash flow in the market at once.

Most people treat this as abstract until they see the historical parallel: in 2022, as the Fed hiked 525 basis points in the fastest tightening cycle in four decades, the Nasdaq fell roughly 33% while high-duration, cash-burning growth names like those in the ARK Innovation ETF fell closer to 67%, more than double the index. The gap wasn't about worse businesses; it was duration mismatch, compounded by multiple compression, as investors paid less for every dollar of future earnings. That's the same lens Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya applied this month, calling Nvidia's roughly 10-times forward earnings multiple a 'generational low' — a statement about how much the market has already repriced for rate risk, not about the chip business deteriorating.

That framework is exactly what to carry into the next two weeks. The December 4 jobs report and the December 9 FOMC decision are the next two data points that can move the discount rate itself, not just sentiment, and futures already price roughly 85-90% odds of a quarter-point hike to 3.75%-4.00%. A hotter payrolls number would likely push yields higher and squeeze long-duration names like Nvidia again, even if today's rebound continues into next week; a softer number could ease hike odds and let growth stocks extend today's bounce. The 10-year yield, not the daily stock tape, is the variable actually transmitting this macro calendar into equity valuations.
